cards.title: Use TKI to Understand Conflict Styles on the Team
cards.summary: The Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument helps team members see their natural conflict inclinations so they can make more strategic choices about which approach fits each situation.
cards.use_when: Team friction is slowing a merchandising, pricing, or vendor-negotiation decision, and the operator wants to help the team choose an appropriate conflict approach rather than defaulting to their habits.
steps: Have team members identify their default conflict mode (competition, collaboration, compromise, avoidance, accommodation) using the TKI or a similar self-assessment.
Use the shared vocabulary to discuss which mode fits the current issue — e.g., a fast pricing response may need competition or compromise, while a vendor agreement may need collaboration.
Pair the assessment with direct conversation so team members see their own resistance patterns and can deliberately choose a more useful approach for the specific decision at hand.
caveats: The source presents the TKI as one helpful tool among several; it is not a prescriptive rule for every conflict.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader Restraint During Team Conflict
cards.summary: Leaders who jump in to protect members from disagreement deprive the team of the chance to develop conflict-management skills; restraint is the harder and more effective choice.
cards.use_when: An operator is tempted to step into a merchandising or marketing disagreement between team members because they fear the conflict is becoming unproductive.
steps: Recognize the urge to protect team members from harm is often a premature interruption of a disagreement that could resolve itself.

Allow resolution to occur naturally even when it looks messy; the source compares overprotection to parents who shield children from sibling quarrels, which strains relationships and leaves people hungry for resolution.
Model appropriate conflict behavior personally — avoiding necessary conflict is the surest way to let the dysfunction thrive.
Accept that losing control of the team during conflict does not mean failing as a leader; it often means the team is building its own capacity.
caveats: The source acknowledges this is difficult; the leader must still intervene if the team truly fails, but that should be a rare occurrence.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Commitment Comes from Clarity and Buy-In, Not Consensus
cards.summary: Great teams make clear, timely decisions and achieve full buy-in even when members disagree, understanding that consensus is not required for support.
cards.use_when: An operator is trying to get the whole team behind a product launch, pricing change, or campaign decision and is tempted to delay until everyone agrees.
steps: Separate the need for buy-in from the desire for consensus: reasonable people do not need to get their way, only to know their opinions were heard and considered.
Ensure everyone's ideas are genuinely aired, then rally around whatever decision the group or leader makes.
When there's an impasse, let the leader make the call rather than forcing false agreement.
Push for closure on clear decisions even without full certainty; the source argues a decision is better than no decision.
Recognize that unresolved commitment gaps at the top multiply into larger alignment problems downstream, especially for teams executing across departments.
caveats: This is the source's philosophy, not a universal rule; some decisions genuinely need more information, and the source still values research and analysis.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Use Cascading Messaging to Align the Team and the Organization
cards.summary: A short end-of-meeting exercise where the team reviews key decisions and agrees what to communicate prevents small executive misalignments from becoming major discrepancies downstream.
cards.use_when: A weekly or quarterly ecommerce team meeting is ending and decisions need to be communicated to store staff, vendors, or cross-functional partners.
steps: At the end of the meeting, spend at least 10 minutes explicitly reviewing the key decisions made.
Agree on what needs to be communicated to employees or other constituencies about each decision.
Identify which decisions should remain confidential and which must be communicated quickly and comprehensively.
Use the exercise to surface misalignment — often team members learn they are not on the same page and clarify outcomes before putting anything into action.
Send a consistent message so employees are not receiving contradictory statements from managers who attended the same meeting.
caveats: The source says the exercise takes a minimum of 10 minutes; skipping it undermines the alignment it is meant to create.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Set and Honor Decision Deadlines
cards.summary: Clear deadlines for decisions — including intermediate milestones — are a primary tool for overcoming commitment dysfunction and preventing costly ambiguity.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team is stalling on a pricing decision, assortment change, or campaign launch and keeps revisiting the same debate.
steps: Set a clear deadline for when each decision will be made, and honor the date with discipline and rigidity.
Commit to deadlines for intermediate decisions and milestones as well as final ones, so misalignment is identified before costs become too great.
Treat timing as a critical part of clarity: ambiguity about when a decision will be made is the biggest enemy of a commitment-prone team.
Review whether the team is honoring deadlines at the start of each meeting, and address missed dates directly.
caveats: Deadlines work only if they are actually honored; a deadline that slips without consequence reinforces the dysfunction.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Worst-Case Scenario and Contingency Planning to Reduce Fear of Deciding
cards.summary: Briefly clarifying the worst-case outcome of a decision lets a hesitant team see that the costs of being wrong are survivable and smaller than imagined.
cards.use_when: A team is frozen on a high-stakes decision such as entering a new channel, launching a major product, or committing to a large marketing spend.
steps: Before or during the decision, briefly discuss contingency plans for what happens if the decision is wrong.
Even better, clarify the worst-case scenario explicitly so the team can see the cost is survivable and less damaging than assumed.
Use this to reduce the fear that is driving delay and paralysis.
Once the worst case is understood, move to closure and commit to the chosen path.
caveats: This is a fear-reduction tool, not a substitute for analysis; it is for teams that overvalue certainty, not for teams that routinely underanalyze decisions.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Low-Risk Exposure Therapy for Commitment-Phobic Teams
cards.summary: Deliberately making decisions in low-risk situations with substantial discussion but little analysis builds the team's confidence and reveals it overvalues lengthy study.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team habitually delays decisions until exhaustive analysis is done, and the operator wants to build the muscle of deciding without perfect information.
steps: Choose a genuinely low-risk decision — a small site change, a minor campaign tweak, a low-stakes vendor choice.
Force a decision after substantial discussion but little additional analysis or research.
Afterward, review the quality of the decision and compare it to what the team expected.
Use the result to show that the decision was not much different from what lengthy study would have produced.
Gradually apply the same confidence to higher-stakes decisions.
caveats: The source explicitly says this is not a claim that research and analysis are unnecessary; teams with this dysfunction tend to overvalue them, which is the problem being corrected.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader's Role in Building Commitment
cards.summary: The leader must be comfortable being wrong, constantly push for closure, and avoid placing too high a premium on certainty or consensus.
cards.use_when: An operator leads a team that keeps deferring decisions and needs to set the tone that bold decisions with course-correction are acceptable.
steps: Accept the prospect of making a decision that ultimately turns out to be wrong, and communicate that acceptance to the team.
Constantly push the group for closure around issues rather than letting discussions continue indefinitely.
Hold the team to the schedules it has set, including intermediate milestones.
Avoid signaling that certainty or consensus is required before a decision can be made.
caveats: The source frames this as the leader's responsibility more than any other member's, but it does not mean the leader decides everything; the point is to create conditions for commitment.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Peer Accountability Over Bureaucratic Performance Management
cards.summary: The most effective way to maintain high standards is peer pressure — team members calling each other on behavior — which reduces the need for excessive bureaucracy.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team has performance or behavior problems and the operator is considering adding new policies or formal corrective processes.
steps: Define accountability as the willingness of team members to call peers on performance or behaviors that might hurt the team.
Encourage team members to 'enter the danger' and have difficult conversations rather than avoid them.
Recognize that close teammates sometimes avoid accountability because they fear damaging the relationship — but the source argues this erodes trust and breeds resentment.
Hold one another accountable to demonstrate respect and high expectations, which the source says strengthens relationships.
Rely on peer pressure as the most efficient way to maintain standards, reducing the need for bureaucratic corrective action.
caveats: This is the source's stated opinion that peer pressure is the most effective and efficient means; it is not a universal rule that formal performance management is never needed.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Publication of Goals and Standards Enables Accountability
cards.summary: Publicly clarifying what the team must achieve, who delivers what, and how everyone must behave makes accountability concrete and removes ambiguity.
cards.use_when: An operator wants to make it easier for team members to hold each other accountable on a new initiative or across a cross-functional project.
steps: Clarify publicly what the team needs to achieve, who needs to deliver what, and how everyone must behave in order to succeed.
Keep the agreements in the open so no one can easily ignore them.
Even after the team has initially committed to a plan or behavioral standards, revisit and re-publish them rather than assuming everyone remembers or agrees.
Use the published goals as the reference point for peer-to-peer feedback and progress reviews.
caveats: The enemy of accountability is ambiguity; if goals and standards stay vague or private, peer accountability is much harder.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Simple and Regular Progress Reviews for Accountability
cards.summary: A little structure goes a long way: regular verbal or written communication about how teammates are doing against stated objectives prevents avoidance of accountability.
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team is not giving each other feedback on performance, and the operator wants a lightweight review rhythm that surfaces problems early.
steps: Set an expectation that team members regularly communicate with one another about how they feel teammates are doing against stated objectives and standards.
Choose a format — verbal or written — and keep it simple and consistent.
Do not rely on team members to do this on their own with no clear expectations or structure; the source says that invites avoidance.
Use the reviews to identify potential problems quickly by questioning one another's approaches without hesitation.
caveats: The source emphasizes structure, not heavy process; the goal is regular, simple reviews rather than a new bureaucratic system.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Team Rewards to Build a Culture of Accountability
cards.summary: Shifting rewards from individual performance to team achievement creates a culture where peers are unlikely to stand by quietly while someone fails to pull their weight.
cards.use_when: An operator is designing incentives for a store team — merchandising, marketing, fulfillment — and wants execution to depend on collective results rather than individual metrics alone.
steps: Shift rewards away from individual performance toward team achievement where the work is genuinely interdependent.
Recognize that when the team shares in the outcome, members are unlikely to stand by quietly and let the team fail because a peer is not pulling their weight.
Combine team rewards with published goals and simple progress reviews so the team knows what the shared standard is.
The leader remains the ultimate arbiter of discipline if the team itself fails, but this should be a rare occurrence.
caveats: The source notes that relying on rewards alone is problematic if it assumes financial motivation is the sole driver of behavior; team rewards are one tool among several.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader's Role: Avoid the Accountability Vacuum
cards.summary: Strong leaders can accidentally become the only source of discipline; the goal is to let the team be the primary accountability mechanism, with the leader as rare final arbiter.
cards.use_when: An operator finds that team members only raise problems to them, not to each other, and wants to shift accountability to the team.
steps: Notice if your own strength as a leader is creating an accountability vacuum — team members may assume the leader will handle discipline, so they hold back.
Actively encourage and allow the team to serve as the first and primary accountability mechanism.
Communicate clearly that accountability is a shared team responsibility, not a consensus approach where anyone can opt out.
Reserve your own intervention as the ultimate arbiter of discipline when the team itself fails — rare, but clear to everyone.
caveats: The source warns that stepping in too often recreates the vacuum; stepping in too little risks the team never developing its own accountability.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Focus on Results, Not Team or Individual Status
cards.summary: The ultimate dysfunction is caring about something other than collective goals; teams get distracted by team status (just belonging) or individual status (personal advancement).
cards.use_when: An ecommerce team seems comfortable but is not hitting growth or profitability goals, or members are optimizing for their own function rather than the store's collective outcome.
steps: Diagnose whether the team is focused on team status — being satisfied by merely belonging to the group — or individual status — enhancing personal position at the expense of the team.
Define specific objectives and clearly defined outcomes, recognizing that results include outcome-based performance, not only financial metrics.
Make the collective results of the group more important to each individual than their own goals.
Watch for symptoms: stagnation, failing to grow, rarely defeating competitors, losing achievement-oriented employees, and being easily distracted.
Address the root cause directly — the source says no amount of trust, conflict, commitment, or accountability can compensate for a lack of desire to win.
caveats: The source's examples include nonprofits, political groups, and prestigious companies that fall into the status trap; the dysfunction is not limited to commercial teams.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Public Declaration of Results
cards.summary: Teams that publicly commit to specific results are more likely to work with a passionate, even desperate desire to achieve them; 'we'll do our best' is a subtle preparation for failure.
cards.use_when: An operator wants a team or the whole store organization to raise its ambition and accountability around a growth or turnaround target.
steps: Define the specific results the team intends to achieve.
Make public proclamations about intended success to the team, the company, or relevant constituencies.
Use the public commitment to focus attention and effort, as the source says teams that commit publicly work harder to achieve the result.
Avoid the soft framing of 'we'll do our best,' which the source says subtly prepares the team for failure.
caveats: The source notes that for athletic teams, public guarantees can unnecessarily provoke opponents; for most teams, public commitment is helpful. It is a motivational tool, not a guarantee of the outcome.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Results-Based Rewards
cards.summary: Tying rewards, especially compensation, to the achievement of specific outcomes keeps attention on results, though relying on this alone assumes financial motivation is the sole driver.
cards.use_when: An operator is setting bonuses or recognition for a team and wants to avoid rewarding effort in the absence of results.
steps: Tie rewards, especially compensation, to the achievement of specific outcomes.
Avoid letting someone take home a bonus merely for 'trying hard' when the result was not achieved, because the source says this signals that achieving the outcome may not be important.
Use rewards as one of several tools, not the only one, since relying on them alone assumes financial motivation is the sole driver of behavior.
Combine with public declaration of results and clear goals so the team understands what outcomes are being rewarded.
caveats: The source explicitly warns that relying on rewards alone is problematic; pair it with other practices.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Leader Sets the Tone for Results Focus
cards.summary: If team members sense the leader values anything other than results, they take that as permission to do the same; leaders must be selfless and objective in rewards and recognition.
cards.use_when: An operator wants to build or repair a results-focused culture and is examining whether their own behavior is reinforcing or undermining it.
steps: Audit what you personally reward and recognize — if it is not results, the team will follow suit.
Be selfless and objective in reserving rewards and recognition for those who make real contributions to the achievement of group goals.
Avoid signaling that status, tenure, or personal relationships matter more than achieving outcomes.
Model the focus on results consistently, since the source says the leader sets the tone more for this dysfunction than for any of the others.
caveats: The source's claim is that the leader sets the tone more for this dysfunction than others; it does not mean the leader alone is responsible for results.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx

cards.title: Kathryn's Meeting Cadence: How Much Time a Strong Team Spends Together
cards.summary: Kathryn's model shows a management team spending roughly eight days per quarter together — fewer than three days per month — which saves time by eliminating confusion and minimizing redundant effort.
cards.use_when: An operator is deciding how much meeting time the management team needs and is weighing 'real work' against structured team time.
steps: Adopt an annual planning meeting and leadership development retreat (three days, off-site) covering budget, strategy, leadership training, succession planning, and cascading messaging.

Hold quarterly staff meetings (two days, off-site) for major goal reviews, financial review, strategic discussions, employee performance, key issue resolution, team development, and cascading messages.
Run weekly staff meetings (two hours, on-site) for key activity review, goal progress, sales review, customer review, tactical issue resolution, and cascading messages.
Schedule ad hoc topical meetings (two hours, on-site) for strategic issues that cannot be adequately discussed in the weekly meeting.
Recognize that spending this time together actually saves time by reducing confusion and redundant communication, even though most management teams resist it.
caveats: The source presents Kathryn's methods as one way to run a management team, not the only way; the numbers are a model, not a universal prescription.
cards.source_name: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.docx
